units.title: What are cryptarithms?
units.description: Meet number puzzles where letters stand in for digits.
learningObjectives: State the rules of cryptarithm puzzles
Set up a cryptarithm as column addition

blocks.text: A **cryptarithm** is a calculation where each digit has been replaced by a letter. Your job is to work out which digit each letter stands for.

blocks.label: A cryptarithm
blocks.description:
A B
+ B A
-----
  8 8 — each letter hides one digit; identical letters mean identical digits.

items: Each letter stands for exactly one digit, and different letters stand for different digits
The first letter of a number cannot be 0
The restored arithmetic must be correct, column by column

blocks.text: Cryptarithms are solved with ordinary column arithmetic plus logical deduction — no guessing races needed.
Read the puzzle column by column, units first. Each column produces a small equation that includes any **carry** flowing in from the right and any carry flowing out to the left.

blocks.question: In a cryptarithm, why can the letter A (as the first digit of AB) never be 0?

options.text: Because then AB would really be a one-digit number B
Because 0 must always stand for the letter O

blocks.explanation: Leading zeros are not written in standard numbers, so a leading letter must stand for a digit from 1 to 9.

units.title: Strategies: columns, carries and parity
units.description: A toolkit of deductions: carry limits, column equations and parity checks.
learningObjectives: Bound the carry entering and leaving each column
Use column equations and parity to deduce digits

blocks.text: When two digits are added, the column sum is at most 9 + 9 + 1(carry) = 19, so the carry leaving any column is at most 1. Knowing this immediately bounds every column equation.

blocks.value: \text{column: } a + b + c_{\text{in}} = c_{\text{out}} \times 10 + r, \qquad c_{\text{out}} \in \{0, 1\}

blocks.title: Worked example: parity in A B + B A = D D

content.text: Expanding, AB + BA = 11 × (A + B). If the result is DD = 11 × D, then A + B = D. So the units digit D equals the sum of the two digits, and the tens column must work out with carry 1.
Parity speeds things up: if the sum DD has both digits even, then 11 × (A + B) being a repdigit of even digits forces A + B even, which happens exactly when A and B have the **same parity**.

blocks.text: Write each column as an equation with its carry, then use bounds, parity and 'different letters, different digits' to eliminate cases.

blocks.question: In AB + B = AAC, what can you say about the carry out of the units column?

options.text: It must be 0, because the units result is C
It must be 1, because A appears in the tens place of the answer while only B was added below
It can be 0 or 1 depending on A
Carries do not exist in cryptarithms

blocks.explanation: The tens column receives B + (carry) + 0 and produces A, and the hundreds digit A also appears — with two addends the only source of a new leading digit is a carry of 1 into the hundreds.

units.title: Classic cryptarithms
units.description: Solve complete puzzles end to end, column by column.

content.text: Units column: B + A ends in 8, so A + B is 8 or 18. Tens column: A + B (the same sum!) plus carry equals 88.

So any pair of different digits A ≠ B with A ≥ 1 and A + B = 8 solves it: A,B ∈ {1,7}, {2,6}, {3,5}, {5,3}, {6,2}, {7,1} — and {4,4} is banned since equal letters cannot differ. Six solutions, all sharing A + B = 8.

blocks.text: The lesson: cryptarithms can have several solutions, and part of the art is describing **all** of them rather than stopping at the first.

blocks.title: Worked example: A A + A = B B B

content.text: AA + A = 11A + A = 12A. We need 12A = 111 × B = BBB with B a digit.

Try B = 2, 3, …: B = 2 gives 12A = 222, so A = 18.5 ✗. B = 4? 444/12 = 37 ✗. No digit A works for any B — checking all B from 1 to 9 shows no solution exists. Some cryptarithms are impossible, and proving impossibility is a valid answer!

blocks.question: For AB + BA = 88, which of the following is a valid assignment?
blocks.explanation: A + B must equal 8 with A ≠ B and A ≥ 1. A = 1, B = 7 gives 17 + 71 = 88 ✓. A = B = 4 breaks the distinct-digits rule; the other pairs sum to 8 but give 80 + 08 = 88 with a leading zero, or 91 + 19 = 110.
